name: Gareth Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play rhythm guitar in a paid folk duo, record simple demo tracks and assist a senior tutor with beginner guitar lessons. I worked the railway ticket desk until a few years ago and have secondary school, not a music qualification; I still miss a chord change if I rush.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What makes a good week at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works part-time at a garden shop and our children are grown. At 58 I would like to know what retirement will pay, but I have not checked; two weeks of expenses saved will not cover a missed run of gigs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the pub owner that software might send a tidy poster, but it cannot hold the room with a steady guitar. I would ask for the gig fee before clearing the evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have two weeks saved and the garden-shop hours change with the season. A cancelled run of pub dates would hurt even if AI stays modest, and there are few paid local bands to join.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would keep the paid duo dates, demo tracks and supervised beginner lessons. I use AI now and then to sort set lists, but I play every proposed change before sending it to the singer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about an ordinary booking gap. The pub can cancel faster than I can replace its fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has a pub cancelled on you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One closed for repairs after we had bought train tickets. I would ask for written cancellation pay and travel costs before another out-of-town booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you rely on a pension soon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not until I get a written estimate. I would keep paid work on the calendar rather than guess.

I would ask for the **gig fee** before clearing the evening.
think: Our **two-week reserve** cannot absorb several lost gigs while food and rent bills keep arriving.
Variable **garden-shop hours** add to the household risk.
do: Keep **paid folk dates**, demos and supervised lessons this month.
Request **written cancellation pay** and travel costs before out-of-town gigs.
Request a **written retirement estimate** while keeping paid work instead of guessing.
feel: I feel **anxious** about existing booking gaps.
S0.quote: The pub can cancel faster than I can replace its fee.
fieldNote: His **late junior start** follows railway work, so he still needs supervision despite years of paid work elsewhere.
The **thin reserve** and seasonal partner hours make ordinary cancellations matter.

steps.text: Keep paid folk duo dates, simple demos and supervised beginner lessons
Request written cancellation and travel pay before out-of-town pub dates
Request written retirement estimate while keeping paid work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the pub owner that generated demos may be cheap, but the audience buys a live evening. I would ask which rehearsals and Friday sets are actually paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Demos are about a quarter of my small music pay, and I expect fewer clients for them. I can learn a tool that has been tested, but I cannot claim a better guitar job by pressing a button.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would ask the duo partner for three months of written paid dates and the recording engineer for a paid lesson on a new timing checker. In the first year I would test only a guitar take I own without client names if the studio approves local storage; I would compare each beat by ear against the original and stop if timing shifts or the file leaves the studio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing demo fees. I can try a proven checker. The human rehearsal still needs a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you test a pupil’s recording?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A child’s name or voice stays out of the tool; I would use my own unlabelled take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Friday sets are cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If paid dates really fall, I would apply for a posted paid venue guitar assistant job only if my secondary schooling and supervised playing qualify, written net pay after travel replaces lost sets and the last train gets me home; I would keep the duo until a signed offer. I would ask to see the written hours before applying.

Apply for a **posted venue role** after lost sets if qualified; written net after travel replaces fees, train fits.
feel: I feel **anxious** about realistic demo-fee loss.
S1.quote: The human rehearsal still needs a wage.

A **venue move** needs actual date cuts, qualified paid posting, written net replacement, train access and signed offer.

Request three months of written paid duo dates and engineer lesson

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the duo that AGI by 2028 may make a demo song before we meet the client. I would ask the pubs to sign the live dates and fees now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect demo sales to end in 2028 and some pubs to buy generated backing instead of a duo. Robots that can handle guitars come around 2031, three years later; the lost demos arrive first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would total demo invoices and request signed paid pub dates. In the first year after 2028, if live duo fees also fall, I would apply for a posted arts-centre guitar aide role only if my schooling and supervised experience qualify, written net pay after travel replaces lost gig fees and the bus home runs; I would keep the duo and lessons until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed if demos and gigs fell together, because that is nearly all my own wage. I have lain awake over the heating bill. Two weeks of savings would not cover the winter heating bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a new recording setup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after a signed paying client order covers the gear and travel. I would not borrow for a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at 60?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 60 in 2028, but I have no written estimate of retirement income. I would ask for one and keep working meanwhile.

S2.quote: Two weeks of savings would not cover the winter heating bill.
fieldNote: His **2028 demo loss** precedes guitar-playing robots around 2031.
The **aide move** needs actual gig loss, qualified posted job, written net pay, home transport and signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the pub owner that five years until AGI by 2031 gives me time to learn the sound desk while live groups still play. I would want a paid training place, not a volunteer badge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Demos may stop paying by 2031, while guitar-playing robots could arrive around 2034. A venue sound job might replace part of my wage if I qualify, but lessons cost time I cannot donate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This autumn I would take a six-month venue-sound certificate only if the theatre offers a real funded place, paid training hours and a timetable that fits the last train without cutting my partner’s shop shifts. In the first year after 2031, if paid demos or gigs fall, I would apply for a posted paid sound-assistant job only if the certificate qualifies me, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the bus home runs; I would keep the duo and supervised pupils until a written offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel anxious about losing demos, though paid training gives me a route. I will not put a course fee on a card at 63.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you operate a crowded show alone after training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The house technician must supervise my first sound checks, and I would not run a crowded night alone until equipment and safety checks are signed off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is free but hours are unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid pub dates and wait for a paid intake. Free tuition would still leave us short of weekly wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the folk duo that ten years until AGI by 2036 gives us time to make paid dates and training clear. I will be 68 then, and applause will still not pay a bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Demo sales may end by 2036, and robots might play the pub around 2039. The present two-week reserve and variable shop hours make this winter the first problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this month I would ask for a written two-year paid duo calendar and save five percent of each extra paid Sunday lesson after food, rent and train fare, aiming for two months. In the first year after 2036 I would keep paid sets and, only if demo or gig fees fall, apply for a posted centre music assistant job only if my schooling qualifies, written net pay after travel covers lost demo and gig fees and transport works; I would leave only after a signed offer states hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay anxious because a decade does not cover next month’s rent. A small savings rule works only when an extra learner pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there are no extra lessons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I save nothing that week. I cannot move rent money into a savings label.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What will retirement actually pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know yet. I would request a written estimate, but I would not give up paid work on a guess.

I would ask the duo to make **training terms** clear.

S4.quote: A small savings rule works only when an extra learner pays.
fieldNote: His **two-month goal** uses extra lesson fees actually paid after essentials.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because demo and live fees might fall before I have more than two weeks of savings. Signed paid pub dates, a qualified posted job and transport home would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens after the last train. A written show fee is only useful if I can get home without spending it.

headlineQuote: A written show fee is only useful if I can get home without spending it.
portrait: At **58**, Gareth is a junior folk guitarist who came from railway ticket work and finished secondary school.
His **lower pay**, two-week reserve and few local jobs make lost pub dates a present risk.
He uses **AI occasionally** and tries a new checker only after paid instruction, approved storage and ear comparison.
A **funded sound course** needs paid hours, transport and no lost partner pay before qualified posted work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase demo fees and cut paid pub dates before another job opens.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed pub dates**, a qualified posted job with written net pay and transport home would help Gareth.
